practice.title: Conscientiousness of Bodhichitta
agreedSteps: Meditate on a strong wish to increase conscientiousness of bodhichitta — the purpose is to prevent our bodhichitta from degenerating, and the contemplation is thinking about the ramifications if it does degenerate (rebirth in lower realms, our ability to benefit others decreases, we become far removed from the bodhisattva grounds).

During the meditation break, maintain mindfulness throughout the day — remembering that catching delusions early, when they are still mild, prevents us from ever having to fight the overwhelming battles we keep losing.
steps: Identify the points in your life where your mind becomes vulnerable to delusions — certain times, environments, or situations — and have a plan ready in advance rather than trying to come up with a strategy in the moment.
Remember that every moment of our life is training: the way we handle washing the dishes, resting, and walking is the very machinery of mind we will bring to the hardest moments of our lives.
practice.quote: I actually just need to improve my mindfulness. That's it.

commentary.title: The Monk, the Goat, and the Slippery Slope
content: A monk in a cave was supported by a family whose daughter secretly wished to seduce him. When she finally presented him with three impossible demands — make love to her, kill a goat, or drink alcohol, threatening suicide if he refused all three — he chose the alcohol as 'the least harmful.' But once drunk, he committed every act he had feared. Not one was left undone. Such is the power of a breach of mindfulness.

As long as we're in samsara, there are countless situations where the only choices are terrible. When those arise, we need to use them — not waste the experience. The problem isn't this person or that situation. The problem is simply that we are in samsara. These impossible scenarios will keep happening, over and over, as long as we remain in contaminated life.
commentary.quote: By giving in a little bit, we are giving in a lot. And basically, we're giving in totally, eventually.

commentary.title: Vows as Protection Against Concession
content: Part of the reason we have vows is that they keep us out of slippery-slope territory. The mental concessions the Maras prey on always begin with 'just this little breach.' But vows draw a line and say: when you go below this, you lose everything. It looks like a little, but the little turns into a little more, into everything.

It's like stepping onto an icy hillside — just a little bit means falling all the way down. Buddha's wisdom is saying: I've been around, I've seen it all. Please take my word for these rules of thumb for living. You have a lot of freedom, but when you go below these lines, it almost always turns into problems.

commentary.title: Self-Conception and the Identity of Defeat
content: When we follow even a small delusion, we create a self-conception of ourselves as someone who follows delusion. Our mind can't tell the difference between 'someone who follows a little delusion' and 'someone who follows delusion.' We create an identity, and that identity is predictive — it results in repeatedly falling, over and over.

There's also a discouragement that sets in. We start telling ourselves: I can't fight my delusions, I don't know how to not follow them, I always give in. That narrative gets reinforced. Then when delusions arise, we feel overwhelmed and quit before the battle even begins.

commentary.title: Delusions Compound Exponentially
content: Following a little attachment makes us a slightly more attached person — and that slightly more attached person is willing to go a bit further. Very quickly we go from 2% attached to 50% to completely maniacal. The more we follow any delusion, the more we follow even more delusions, and they breed and support each other.

More attachment creates more anger, because we become rigid about wanting things we can't get. More anger creates more unhappiness, which drives more attachment as we try to escape the pain. More attachment creates more impatience and aversion. It compounds more and more. What looked like 'just a little delusion' is actually giving in totally.

commentary.title: Fight the Battle Ten Days Earlier
content: When we follow a delusion, the real battle was usually lost ten steps earlier — when our mindfulness first got weak. We can trace it back. The strong rage didn't come from nowhere; it came days after we'd already been feeding forms of anger and non-acceptance.

What gets us discouraged is fighting the battle when the delusion is already full-blown, when it absolutely destroys us. But if instead we focus on improving our mindfulness and vigilance against even the slightest subtle forms of delusion developing, we prevent the slippery slopes from forming at all. Then it's just: mild annoyance coming up, cool, I know how to work with that. Mild craving, interesting, I can handle that. That area of working with our mind is actually easy and comfortable.
This is so empowering. We don't need to fight raging behemoths of delusion. We just need to improve our mindfulness — and that's it.
commentary.quote: I actually just need to improve my mindfulness. That's it. And we'll feel very blessed and inspired and think [...] that's what I got to do.

commentary.title: No Expectations of Reasonableness
content: The story of Shariputra, who developed bodhichitta and then abandoned it when a demon behaved unreasonably, carries an important practical teaching. As we train as bodhisattvas, we need to have no expectation of reasonableness from anyone — zero. If we have even 1% expectation, we'll constantly be annoyed.

We need to think: I am in it for the long haul. People aren't going to be thankful. They're sometimes going to spit in my face. That doesn't matter. What I'm in it for is not about little bits of praise or dopamine hits. No matter what, I'm doing it. If I'm getting into a critical mindset, judging and scorning others — that's my problem, not theirs. I can't expect deluded beings to be reasonable. We're not reasonable either.

commentary.title: Conscientiousness Versus Mindfulness
content: Conscientiousness is a strong determination to abandon non-virtue and practice virtue — it's a state of mind that thinks: non-virtue, bad; virtue, good. Mindfulness is the part of the mind that remembers something previously known and functions to not forget it. They work in tandem: conscientiousness provides the why, and mindfulness provides the remembering.

If conscientiousness is like understanding all the reasons to take care of your physical health, mindfulness of virtue is like actually working out. Some people start taking care of themselves without the why, and they burn out. With a powerful why — really seeing the value of virtue and the faults of delusion — our moral discipline practice is naturally much stronger.

commentary.title: Vulnerability and Planning
content: We should all be aware of where we're vulnerable — what situations, people, environments make our mind susceptible. The distant cause is always a lack of mindfulness. But there are immediate causes too, like tiredness.

Where we can't attack the cause, we need a plan ready in advance. For the 3:30 a.m. wake-up when the Maras attack: improve the Yoga of Sleep practice, and have a response ready for the second we wake up — automatically start the Liberating Prayer, or recite Vajrasattva's mantra, or begin the Heart Sutra. The idea is a strategy we can enact without needing to brainstorm while exhausted.

Every moment really counts. What we do with our mind in each moment — walking, resting, washing the dishes — is exactly what we'll do with our mind when we're grieving, dealing with sickness, or facing the biggest losses of our life. There's no insignificant moment.
commentary.quote: The way I wash the dishes is the way that I'm going to grieve. The way that I rest is going to be the way that I deal with cancer one day.

dataShares: Suzanne stepped in to teach a class for the first time on a few hours' notice, learning to rely on her spiritual guide and finding that being thrown into the deep end was actually the best way to finally do it.

Anne intensified her cessation-of-distractions project with daily meditation, Vajrasattva purification, all-day dedication, an accountability partner, and a tracking spreadsheet — but hadn't noticed a big shift yet after six weeks.
Alexis resonated with the teaching on non-discouragement, recognizing the anxiety of doing the practice and not seeing results, and the importance of not grasping at outcomes.

Adriana attended her 30th high school reunion focused on cherishing others and purifying karma, and discovered that her own pride — always trying to be the best — was likely the real cause of her social difficulties.

Sumit experienced attachment at a wedding and used Dharma reasoning to feel better, but questioned whether he was truly practicing emptiness or just using a temporary opponent like a cough suppressant.
